newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranian President Khatami pledges domestic reform.
newsitem.headline: Iranian President Khatami pledges domestic reform.

text.p: Iranian President Mohammad Khatami has pledged to carry out wide-ranging domestic reforms despite early signs that he will face stern opposition from conservative opponents in parliament.

Swept to power in a landslide election victory in May, the 54-year-old moderate Moslem Shi'ite cleric has not backed away from his promises to introduce greater social and economic freedoms in the 18-year-old Islamic Republic.
"I have a pact with the people to fulfil my plans," he said on Wednesday in a televised interview.
Khatami committed himself to improving the economy, allowing the creation of formal political parties and encouraging an independent press.
"To provide channels to convey peoples' needs to the state we need organised political parties, social associations and an independent free press," Khatami said.
"The government must eliminate obstacles in...expanding these institutions," he said.

Political parties have been banned since Iran's1979 revolution and the government has kept a tight grip on media freedoms, but factions loyal to the Islamic state have been allowed to set up political organisations and religious associations.

Iran's large youth population, women and the growing middle- class propelled Khatami to office on expectations that he could usher in a host of changes including the relaxation of stern Islamic dress codes.
He said he had chosen a woman vice president, the first since the revolution, in a sign that he was determined to fulfil at least some of those hopes.
But crucial to his programme will be the conservative- dominated Majlis or parliament, which has to approve his cabinet nominees and their planned legislative programmes.

Conservative deputies have already begun to question a key core of the president's moderate candidates, most notably his proposed culture minister Ataollah Mohajerani and interior minister nominee Abdollah Nouri.
The post of culture and Islamic guidance plays a crucial role in daily Iranian life since it has broad powers over what books and films can be produced and the extent of press freedom.
Mohajerani has been singled out by some hardliners in parliament for his past advocacy of greater cultural freedoms and direct talks with the United States in 1990.

"Mohajerani does not deserve to be a member of the cabinet. One who has been the inventor of direct talks with America is detrimental to the foreign image of the government," the conservative Resalat evening paper said.
"We will have to clear up his mess (if appointed)," the paper said in a stinging editorial.

Parliament begins the debate on Khatami's cabinet on August 19 and the final composition of the cabinet is seen as vital in setting the tone and reforming scope of the president's four- year term in office.
But a potential clash with parliament has led some analysts to predict that Khatami will have to take a low-key and gradual approach to carrying out sensitive reforms.

"I don't think that Mr Khatami is going to be able to perform the miracles the people expect of him. I'm rather worried about the next four years," rightist deputy Ahmad Rasool-Nejad told the Iran News daily paper.
Ultimate power in the country of 60 million people, particularly over its foreign relations, rests firmly in the hands of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
